nameStory: This tiny beetle gets its name from two key behaviors: it specializes in eating sumac plants (Rhus species) and can jump like a flea when startled. The 'flea beetle' part comes from its amazing ability to catapult jump up to 100 times its own body length using powerful hind legs, just like a flea escaping danger.
description: The sumac flea beetle is a small, cream-colored beetle about a quarter-inch long with irregular reddish-brown patches across its back. It belongs to the leaf beetle family and specializes in feeding on sumac plants throughout New England. Both the adults and their gray, yellow-striped larvae can be found munching on sumac leaves during the growing season. Despite their tiny size, these beetles are remarkable jumpers that will leap away at the slightest disturbance.

idTips.label: Jumping ability
idTips.description: When disturbed, these beetles spring away with impressive leaps that can carry them 100 times their body length - watch for this distinctive escape behavior

idTips.label: Size and shape
idTips.description: About a quarter-inch long with a compact, oval body typical of leaf beetles - small enough to sit comfortably on your pinky nail

idTips.label: Adult coloration
idTips.description: Cream or pale yellow base color decorated with irregular reddish-brown markings that create a mottled appearance

idTips.label: Host plant association
idTips.description: Almost always found on or near sumac plants - look for them on the leaves of staghorn sumac, smooth sumac, or poison sumac

idTips.label: Larval appearance
idTips.description: Gray larvae with bright yellow stripes that carry a distinctive 'fecal shield' - a mass of their own waste on their backs for protection

habitat: Look for sumac flea beetles wherever sumac plants grow in New England - along roadsides, forest edges, abandoned fields, and disturbed areas. They're particularly common around staghorn sumac thickets in sunny, well-drained locations from sea level to moderate elevations. Since they depend entirely on sumac plants for food and reproduction, their presence is a reliable indicator that Rhus species are nearby.

seasonality.spring: Adults emerge and begin feeding on newly sprouting sumac leaves. Look for small holes and feeding damage on fresh foliage as temperatures warm.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when both adults and larvae are actively feeding on sumac leaves. Larvae with their distinctive fecal shields are most visible during mid to late summer.
seasonality.fall: Adults prepare for winter by seeking shelter while larvae complete development. Feeding activity decreases as sumac leaves begin to change color and drop.
seasonality.winter: Adults overwinter in leaf litter, under bark, or in other protected locations. No visible activity during the cold months.

funFact: The larvae carry around a shield made of their own poop! This 'fecal shield' is packed with toxic chemicals absorbed from sumac leaves, creating a portable chemical weapon that makes them taste terrible to birds and other predators.
confusionNotes: Other small flea beetles can look similar, but most don't have the distinctive cream and reddish coloration or the strong association with sumac plants. Remember: if it's jumping off sumac leaves and has that mottled cream-and-red pattern, it's likely your sumac specialist.
contextualKnowledge: While this beetle feeds on sumac plants, it typically doesn't cause significant damage to established plants. The relationship is more of a natural partnership - the beetle gets food and chemical protection, while the sumac usually tolerates the feeding without serious harm.
compareHints: Since this is the only Blepharida species in our region, compare it to other flea beetles in the leaf beetle family. Most other flea beetles are darker (often metallic green, blue, or black) and lack the distinctive cream base color with reddish markings. The strong association with sumac plants also sets it apart from most other flea beetles, which feed on different host plants.
